documents.prompt: {{item1}} sales and {{item2}} incidents both rise during hot months. Which explanation best shows why correlation does not establish causation?

solutionReview.headline: Hot weather drives both {{item1}} sales and {{item2}} incidents, so their correlation is not evidence of causation.
reasoning: The data show a correlation: in hot months {{item1}} sales go up, and {{item2}} incidents go up too.

Hot weather is a third, lurking variable that affects each one directly: heat raises {{item1}} sales, and heat also leads to more {{item2}} incidents (more people outdoors, in the water, or exposed to the heat).
So the two can rise together even if {{item1}} sales have no effect at all on {{item2}} incidents. The correlation alone cannot show that either one causes the other.
That rules out “the first variable must cause the second” and its reverse, and correlated variables are not identical; they only change together.
solutionReview.commonError: Reading “they rise together” as “one causes the other”. Both could simply be tracking the season.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Hot weather can influence both variables: it raises {{item1}} sales and {{item2}} incidents, so their correlation does not show causation.

attemptFeedback: Use the given information to identify the relationship before computing.
supportHints: Name what each number represents, then choose the operation or relationship that connects them.

choices.label: hot weather can influence both variables
the first variable must cause the second
the second variable must cause the first
correlation proves the variables are identical

documents.prompt: Researchers have {{group}} students and want to know whether a tutoring program CAUSES higher scores. Which design gives the strongest causal evidence?

solutionReview.headline: Only random assignment of the {{group}} students makes the tutoring and no-tutoring groups comparable.
reasoning: To show tutoring CAUSES higher scores, the two groups must differ only in tutoring. Randomly split the {{group}} students, for example {{g1}} to tutoring and {{g2}} to no tutoring, then compare their scores.

Random assignment spreads motivation, prior grades and other lurking variables evenly between the groups on average, so a score difference can be credited to tutoring. That is the Experiment row of the table.
Surveying students who already chose tutoring uses self-selected groups (the Observation row): students who sign up may already be more motivated.
Comparing with a different school last year changes the students and the year as well as the tutoring, and asking whether tutoring felt helpful measures opinions, not scores.
solutionReview.commonError: Trusting a comparison of students who chose tutoring. Their own choice, not the tutoring, could explain higher scores.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Randomly assign participants to tutoring and no-tutoring groups, for example {{g1}} and {{g2}} of the {{group}} students, and compare their scores.

attemptFeedback: Use the given information to identify the relationship before computing.
supportHints: Name what each number represents, then choose the operation or relationship that connects them.

choices.label: randomly assign participants to tutoring and no-tutoring groups
survey students who already chose tutoring
compare this year with a different school last year
ask students whether tutoring felt helpful

documents.prompt: A survey of {{n}} students finds that those who report {{habit}} also report higher grades. What can the survey establish by itself?

solutionReview.headline: A survey of {{n}} students can show that {{habit}} and higher grades go together, not that one causes the other.
reasoning: The researchers only recorded what the {{n}} students reported; nobody was assigned to {{habit}}. That makes it an observational study.
What it can establish: an association. Students who report {{habit}} tend to report higher grades.
What it cannot establish: causation. A lurking variable such as motivation or family support could lead to both {{habit}} and higher grades, or the direction could run the other way.
Surveying more than {{n}} students would not fix this, and nothing in a survey shows that no lurking variables exist. Only a design such as random assignment can rule them out.
solutionReview.commonError: Treating the pattern as proof: students who report {{habit}} having higher grades does not mean {{habit}} causes the higher grades.
solutionReview.answerSummary: An association, not causation: the survey of {{n}} students links {{habit}} with higher grades but cannot show that {{habit}} causes them.

attemptFeedback: Use the given information to identify the relationship before computing.
supportHints: Name what each number represents, then choose the operation or relationship that connects them.

choices.label: an association, not causation
that the habit definitely causes higher grades
that grades cause the habit
that no lurking variables exist

documents.prompt: A headline incorrectly claims, “People who {{behavior}} have {{pct}}% better outcomes, so {{behavior}} causes improvement.” What is the main flaw if the data came only from an observational study?

solutionReview.headline: A {{pct}}% gap from an observational study shows an association; the headline wrongly turns it into causation.
reasoning: The study only observed people who {{behavior}} and people who do not, and found {{pct}}% better outcomes in the first group. That is an association.
People who choose to {{behavior}} may differ in other ways, such as motivation, health or free time, that also improve outcomes. Those confounders could produce the {{pct}}% gap by themselves.
So “{{behavior}} causes improvement” is not supported: the headline confuses association with causation. Showing causation needs a design such as random assignment.
The other options fail: comparing the percentages is fine, the study did show a pattern, and no rule requires exactly 100 people.
solutionReview.commonError: Accepting a large percentage as proof of a cause. Even a {{pct}}% difference can come entirely from who chose to {{behavior}}.
solutionReview.answerSummary: It confuses association with causation: the {{pct}}% gap shows that people who {{behavior}} do better, not that the behavior causes it.

attemptFeedback: Use the given information to identify the relationship before computing.
supportHints: Name what each number represents, then choose the operation or relationship that connects them.

choices.label: it confuses association with causation
percentages can never be compared
observational data can never show any pattern
the sample must have exactly 100 people

variants.prompt: An observational study finds that students who {{behavior}} report {{pct}}% better outcomes. The headline says {{behavior}} CAUSED the improvement. Two explanations are proposed: (A) the behavior itself causes the improvement; (B) a third variable such as prior motivation affects both the behavior and the outcome. Evaluate what the observational study can establish, identify why both explanations remain possible, and choose the evidence that would most strengthen a causal claim.

responseFields.label: What can the observational study establish by itself?

choices.label: An association between the behavior and the outcome
That the behavior definitely caused the outcome

responseFields.label: Why can't Explanation A be selected over B from this study alone?

choices.label: The design does not rule out confounding or pre-existing differences.
Because percentages cannot be used in observational studies.

responseFields.label: Which follow-up would most strengthen causation if ethical?

choices.label: Randomly assign comparable participants to the behavior or a control condition and compare outcomes.
Repeat the same observational survey with more people but no design change.

solutionReview.headline: The {{pct}}% result supports an association; only a design like random assignment can separate explanation A from B.
reasoning: Establish: the study observed students who {{behavior}} reporting {{pct}}% better outcomes, so it shows an association between the behavior and the outcome, not that the behavior definitely caused it.

Why A cannot be chosen over B: prior motivation could lead students both to {{behavior}} and to better outcomes. Both explanations predict the same {{pct}}% gap, because the design does not rule out confounding or pre-existing differences.
Percentages are not the problem; observational studies use them all the time. The problem is that the students chose their own behavior.

Strengthen: randomly assign comparable participants to {{behavior}} or a control condition and compare outcomes. Random assignment balances motivation between the groups; a bigger survey with the same design would still leave B open.
solutionReview.commonError: Picking explanation A because it matches the headline. The {{pct}}% gap is equally consistent with B until the behavior is assigned at random.
solutionReview.answerSummary: An association between the behavior and the outcome; the design does not rule out confounding or pre-existing differences; randomly assign comparable participants to the behavior or a control condition and compare outcomes.

attemptFeedback: Ask what alternative explanation could produce the same observed association.
supportHints: A causal claim is strongest when the treatment/exposure is assigned rather than merely observed.

documents.prompt: A strong association is found between {{x}} and {{y}}. Which follow-up most improves evidence for causation when an experiment is ethical?

solutionReview.headline: To test whether {{x}} causes better {{y}}, assign it at random and compare.
reasoning: The strong association between {{x}} and {{y}} could come from who uses {{x}}: for example, more motivated students may both choose it and do better.
A randomized controlled experiment removes that problem: randomly assign comparable students either to use {{x}} or not, then measure {{y}} for both groups under the same conditions.
Random assignment balances motivation and other lurking variables between the groups on average, so a difference in {{y}} can be attributed to {{x}}.
The other options do not help: collecting the same correlation again repeats the same confounding, and choosing only high-outcome participants or removing low values biases the data.
solutionReview.commonError: Thinking more of the same observational data proves a cause. Repeating the correlation between {{x}} and {{y}} never separates {{x}} from the lurking variables.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Use a randomized controlled experiment: randomly assign students to use {{x}} or not, and compare their {{y}}.

attemptFeedback: Use the given information to identify the relationship before computing.
supportHints: Name what each number represents, then choose the operation or relationship that connects them.

choices.label: use a randomized controlled experiment
collect the same correlation again
choose only participants with high outcomes
remove all low data values

variants.prompt: An observational study finds that students who use {{x}} have higher {{y}}. A second study randomly assigns comparable students either to use {{x}} or to use the usual method, then measures {{y}} under the same conditions. Evaluate what EACH study can support and decide which evidence is needed for a causal claim.

responseFields.label: What can the observational study establish by itself?

choices.label: An association, but not a causal conclusion by itself.
Definitive causation.
It reduces systematic confounding and provides much stronger evidence for causation.
It adds no information beyond the observational association.

responseFields.label: Which study should carry the causal claim when the experiment is ethical and well-run?

choices.label: The randomized comparison study.
The observational study alone.
Random assignment helps separate the treatment effect from pre-existing differences and confounders.
Causation follows simply because one study reports a larger numerical difference.

solutionReview.headline: The observational study shows that {{x}} and higher {{y}} go together; the randomized study can carry a causal claim.
reasoning: Observational study: students chose whether to use {{x}}, so it shows an association with higher {{y}} but not a causal conclusion by itself. The users may differ in motivation or prior skill.

Randomized study: comparable students were randomly assigned to {{x}} or the usual method, and {{y}} was measured under the same conditions. That reduces systematic confounding and provides much stronger evidence for causation.
So the randomized comparison study should carry the causal claim, provided it is ethical and well-run.
Why: random assignment helps separate the treatment effect from pre-existing differences and confounders. A bigger numerical difference in one study is not, by itself, a reason to infer a cause.
solutionReview.commonError: Letting the study with the more impressive {{y}} difference carry the claim. What matters is how the groups were formed.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Observational: an association, but not a causal conclusion by itself. Randomizing: it reduces systematic confounding and strengthens evidence. Claim: the randomized comparison study; it helps separate the treatment effect from confounders.

attemptFeedback: Separate the numerical relationship from the design used to create the groups.
supportHints: Ask whether participants chose their own exposure or were randomly assigned.
